Here's a confession: the most important thing I learned in my thesis wasn't a new model.
It was how to **test** one.

## The trap

Imagine you have several plots of each potato variety. If you split plots into training and
test sets at random, the same variety ends up on both sides. The model can learn
*"variety X looks like this"* instead of *"blight looks like this"*, and the score looks great.

![Random splits leak varieties; grouped splits don't.](../../projects/potato-late-blight/validation.svg){fig-alt="Diagram comparing random and grouped splits"}

## The fix

Group the folds **by variety**, so every variety in the test set is brand new to the model.
Then add a **permutation test** (shuffle the labels and see whether the model still "works") to check the
signal is real and not luck.

## What happened

My score went down. On the test flight the model reached a macro-F1 of 0.394 against a
0.308 baseline. That's small, but it's **real** (p = 0.004), and it's the number someone could
actually expect on new varieties.

## Three takeaways

1. **Ask what "new data" means for your problem** (new plots? new varieties? new fields?) and split that way.
2. **Always compare to a dumb baseline.** "Always predict healthy" was surprisingly hard to beat.
3. **Check your labels.** Replicates of the same variety disagreed 35.8% of the time, which caps any model.

Honest numbers are less flashy, but they're the ones you can build on.
